titleText.es: ¿PENSÁIS QUE ESTO ES COSA DE BROMA?
titleText.en: DO YOU ALL THINK THIS IS A JOKE?
titleText.noteEn: Pensáis is the informal plural “you” form used mainly in Spain.

regions.labelEs: LA SEÑORITA LENHART NO HA PODIDO VENIR HOY, ASÍ QUE ME HA PEDIDO QUE LA SUSTITUYA.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is a person's surname, not a Spanish lexical item to study.

applications.explanationEn: Ha is the third-person present form of the helper haber, and podido is poder's completed-action form.
Podido carries the ability meaning, while venir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Así and que combine here as the result connector.
Ha supplies the present helper and pedido is pedir's completed-action form.
Pedido introduces a request; que leads into sustituya, the special form used for the requested action.

excludedUnits.rationale: This chalkboard label uses an English honorific and a surname, not Spanish vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: HE REPARTIDO VUESTROS EXÁMENES. PODÉIS COMENZAR.

applications.explanationEn: He is the first-person present helper and repartido is repartir's completed-action form.
Vuestros is the masculine plural possessive used for things belonging to the informal plural group being addressed.
The -éis ending marks the informal plural people being addressed in Spain.
Podéis changes for the addressed group, while comenzar remains in its dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: SEÑOR MUNROE, LA SEÑORITA LENHART NO NOS HA ENSEÑADO ESTO.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is a person's surname, not a Spanish lexical item to study.
This is a person's surname, not a Spanish lexical item to study.

applications.explanationEn: Ha is the third-person present helper, followed by enseñado, enseñar's completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: ESO ES PORQUE LA SEÑORITA LENHART NO ENTIENDE LA IMPORTANCIA DE CIERTO TIPO DE MATEMÁTICAS.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is a person's surname, not a Spanish lexical item to study.

applications.explanationEn: Es and que form the conversational lead-in before the student's hesitant objection.

regions.labelEs: ESTO ES MÁS IMPORTANTE QUE CUALQUIER OTRA COSA QUE HAYÁIS APRENDIDO.

applications.explanationEn: Más raises the degree of importante, and the first que introduces what it is compared with.

applications.exampleEs: CUALQUIER OTRA COSA QUE HAYÁIS APRENDIDO
applications.explanationEn: Cualquier leaves the thing open-ended; the later que introduces hayáis aprendido in the special form used for that indefinite set.
The -áis ending identifies the informal plural people addressed in Spain; this particular form is used inside the open-ended clause.
Sin excludes the plural noun peros, treating objections as the “buts” that are not allowed.

regions.labelEs: ES CUESTIÓN DE VIDA O MUERTE.

applications.exampleEs: ES CUESTIÓN DE VIDA O MUERTE
applications.explanationEn: Es supplies the form of ser, followed by the complete fixed expression cuestión de vida o muerte.

excludedUnits.rationale: This horizontal form blank is a place to write an answer, not a Spanish word.

regions.labelEs: 1. El velocirraptor te divisa a 40 metros de distancia y ataca, acelerando a 4 m/s^2 hasta su velocidad punta de 25 m/s. Cuando te ve, echas a correr, alcanzando rápidamente tu velocidad máxima de 6 m/s. ¿Cuánta distancia puedes cubrir hasta ser atrapado y devorado?

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the exercise number, not a Spanish lexical word.
This is a numerical distance value, not a Spanish lexical word.
This is a numerical acceleration with unit symbols, not Spanish vocabulary.
This is a numerical speed with unit symbols, not Spanish vocabulary.
This is a numerical speed with unit symbols, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Acelerando adds the simultaneous action that describes how the attack proceeds.
Velocidad and punta form the established technical combination for a maximum attainable speed.
Echas and a introduce the sudden beginning, while correr names the action that begins.
Alcanzando adds a simultaneous action in the unchanged -ando form.
Cuánta carries a written accent because it directly asks about an amount.
Puedes changes for informal singular “you,” while cubrir stays in its dictionary form.
Ser introduces the passive pattern; atrapado and devorado are the two completed-action forms applied to the person.

regions.labelEs: 2. Estás en el centro de un triángulo equilátero con un velocirraptor en cada esquina. El velocirraptor superior tiene una pata herida por lo que su velocidad máxima está limitada a 10 m/s.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the exercise number, not a Spanish lexical word.
This is a numerical speed with unit symbols, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Por lo que points back to the injured leg and introduces the consequence that follows.
Está describes the current state, limitada agrees with the feminine noun velocidad, and a introduces the numerical limit.
No negates the technical label a escala, warning that the drawing's proportions are not literal.

regions.labelEs: Los raptores correrán hacia ti. ¿En qué ángulo debes correr para maximizar el tiempo que permanecerás vivo?

applications.explanationEn: Correr keeps its complete dictionary form and adds -án for what they will do.
Qué keeps its written accent because it asks for the angle directly.
Debes changes for informal singular “you,” and correr remains in its dictionary form.
Para introduces the purpose, and maximizar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Permanecer keeps its complete dictionary form and adds -ás for what informal singular “you” will do.

regions.labelEs: 3. Los raptores pueden abrir puertas, pero los retrasan. Utilizando el plano de la próxima página, planifica una ruta a través del edificio, suponiendo que los raptores tardan 5 minutos en abrir la primera puerta, y divide el tiempo por la mitad para cada puerta subsiguiente. Recuerda, los raptores corren a 10 m/s y no conocen el miedo.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the exercise number, not a Spanish lexical word.
This is a numerical duration value, not a Spanish lexical word.
This is a numerical speed with unit symbols, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Pueden changes for the plural subject, while abrir stays in its dictionary form.
Utilizando names the means used for the instruction that follows.
Planifica is the positive informal singular command of planificar.
A través de is present here with de contracted together with el as del.
Suponiendo que introduces the working assumption used for the route calculation.
Tardan changes for the plural subject, 5 minutos gives the duration, en links it to abrir, and abrir stays in its dictionary form.
Divide is the positive informal singular command of dividir.
Por la mitad gives the equal-half result of the preceding command divide.
Recuerda is the positive informal singular command of recordar, with the stem change from o to ue.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone asks another person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of pedir, then que, then a special requested-action form of the other verb.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls that special form the subjunctive. It shows that the action is requested rather than stated as a fact. For example, viene means “comes,” but venga is the requested form in pedir que venga. The form after que changes for the person who is supposed to act.

example.en: Ana asks Luis to come.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: I replace her; I stand in for her (as a requested action)
your (informal plural, before masculine plural things)

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.answerEn: you all can; you all may (informal plural)

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

example.en: This is difficult.

cards.answerEn: the comic turns an ordinary math exam into planning for a velociraptor attack
cards.noteEn: The joke treats kinematics, geometry, route planning, and the movie-like danger of clever raptors as urgently practical school material.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que

cards.questionEn: How can you introduce an explanation, excuse, or hesitant objection?
cards.answerEn: Start with es que, then give the explanation.
cards.noteEn: Es que often softens what comes next, especially when the speaker is explaining a problem or pushing back politely. The phrase functions as a unit; its meaning is not obtained by translating es and que separately.

example.es: No puedo ir; es que trabajo esta tarde.
example.en: I can't go; the thing is, I work this afternoon.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing is more of a certain quality than another?
cards.answerEn: Put más before the describing word and que before the other thing.
cards.noteEn: The describing word is an adjective, such as alto for “tall” or importante for “important.” Más raises the degree, and que introduces what you compare it with.

example.es: Este libro es más corto que aquel.
example.en: This book is shorter than that one.

cards.answerEn: Use the subjunctive after que when describing that unknown person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Spanish treats a known person differently from one you are still trying to find. Conozco a alguien que habla inglés means “I know someone who speaks English.” Busco a alguien que hable inglés uses hable because no particular person has been identified.
cards.questionEn: Which verb form do you use when you are looking for a person or thing that has not been identified—and may not exist?

example.es: Busco a alguien que hable inglés.
example.en: I am looking for someone who speaks English.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: you all have (informal plural, in a non-factual or open-ended clause)

cards.questionEn: How can you reject further objections with “no buts”?
cards.noteEn: Pero normally means “but.” Spanish can turn it into the plural noun peros for objections or excuses, so sin peros literally treats those “buts” as things that are not allowed.

example.en: Do it now, no buts.

cards.promptEs: ser cuestión de vida o muerte
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is a matter of life and death?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ser followed by cuestión de vida o muerte.
cards.noteEn: Cuestión de introduces what kind of matter is at stake. Vida o muerte is a fixed contrast used for an extremely serious or urgent situation.

example.es: Para ellos, es cuestión de vida o muerte.
example.en: For them, it is a matter of life and death.

cards.answerEn: at (introducing a measured distance, speed, or rate)

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

example.en: She came in running.

cards.answerEn: Velocity describes motion; acceleration describes how quickly velocity changes.
cards.noteEn: A speed can be measured in meters per second. An acceleration in meters per second squared says how much that speed changes each second.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to the highest speed something can reach?
cards.noteEn: Punta often means a point or tip, but after velocidad it forms the established technical combination velocidad punta. Máxima velocidad is another way to express a maximum speed.

example.es: El tren alcanza su velocidad punta.
example.en: The train reaches its top speed.

cards.answerEn: you start off (in echas a correr)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone suddenly starts running?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of echar or echarse, then a, then correr.
cards.noteEn: In this expression, echar does not keep its usual sense of throwing. The whole pattern marks the sudden beginning of running. Both echar a correr and echarse a correr are used.

example.es: Al oír el ruido, Pablo echó a correr.
example.en: When Pablo heard the noise, he started running.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)
Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action is done to someone or something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ser, then the verb's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls that completed-action form a past participle, often ending in -ado or -ido. In this passive pattern it changes to match the person or thing: atrapado for one masculine person, atrapada for one feminine person, and plural forms ending in -ados or -adas.

example.en: The letter was sent yesterday.

cards.answerEn: a triangle with three equal sides and three equal 60-degree angles
cards.noteEn: Because all three sides and angles match, an equilateral triangle is symmetric around its center. That symmetry matters in distance and path problems.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por lo que

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a fact to its consequence with “so” or “which is why”?
cards.answerEn: Use por lo que before the consequence.
cards.noteEn: Por lo que looks back at the fact just mentioned and introduces what follows from it. The three words work together as one result connector.

example.es: Perdí el autobús, por lo que llegué tarde.
example.en: I missed the bus, which is why I arrived late.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por lo que

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is restricted to a particular amount or option?
cards.answerEn: Use estar, then limitado or limitada to match the thing, then a before the limit.
cards.noteEn: Limitado changes to agree with the thing being described: limitado for a masculine singular noun and limitada for a feminine singular noun. Only estar changes for person and time; a introduces what the restriction allows.

example.es: La entrada está limitada a dos personas.
example.en: Entry is limited to two people.

cards.questionEn: How do you label a drawing whose sizes are not in their true proportions?
cards.answerEn: Write no a escala, meaning “not to scale.”
cards.noteEn: A escala says that the dimensions follow a fixed proportion. Adding no warns that lengths and distances in the drawing should not be compared literally.

example.es: Este mapa no está a escala.
example.en: This map is not to scale.

cards.answerEn: to; at (part of no a escala, “not to scale”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.

example.en: You should call Marta.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to maximize; to make as large as possible
you will remain; you will stay
they can; they are able to

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.en: Open the window.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; part of a través de (“through”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something goes or can be seen through something?
cards.answerEn: Use a través de before the thing: it means “through” or “across.”
cards.noteEn: Keep all three parts together. Before masculine singular el, de and el combine as del: a través del bosque. Before a feminine noun, use a través de la, as in a través de la ventana. The expression can describe literal passage or a figurative means.

example.es: La luz entra a través de la ventana.
example.en: The light comes in through the window.

cards.answerEn: part of a través de, “through” or “across”

cards.noteEn: Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.

example.en: I’m coming from the market.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce an assumption with “assuming that…”?
cards.answerEn: Use suponiendo que before the assumption.
cards.noteEn: Suponiendo que sets a condition or fact that the speaker temporarily accepts for the discussion or calculation. It can introduce either a realistic working assumption or a hypothetical one; the verb form after que depends on how the assumption is presented.

example.es: Suponiendo que llega a tiempo, empezamos a las ocho.
example.en: Assuming that she arrives on time, we start at eight.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long someone takes to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tardar, the amount of time, en, and the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Tardar changes for who takes the time. En links the time to the action and normally has no separate English word in this pattern.

example.en: I take ten minutes to arrive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links the time taken to the action

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an amount is cut or divided in half?
cards.answerEn: Use por la mitad after the verb.
cards.noteEn: Mitad means “half.” With verbs such as dividir, reducir, or cortar, por la mitad says that the result consists of two equal parts; it is understood as “in half,” not as a literal instruction to divide by one-half.

example.es: Cortó la manzana por la mitad.
example.en: She cut the apple in half.

cards.answerEn: they know; they are familiar with
